summary:
Corey Gallon opens by recounting that OpenAI threatened to ban his account while preparing this talk on web automation. His central premise is that a browser controlled via the Chrome DevTools Protocol is indistinguishable from a human user to sites like Google and Cloudflare, because the agent's clicks and keystrokes travel the same internal path as a real user's mouse and keyboard. He structures the methodology around three components: a shell-based CLI rather than an MCP server, the CDP protocol via his open-source Chrome Agent tool, and a sense-act-verify loop climbed up a three-rung ladder only as high as a page forces.

He defends the CLI choice with a study showing parity in capability (~83% success) but massive gaps in round trips (7 vs 71), time (under 1 minute vs 8 minutes), and token cost (up to 75x cheaper per Anthropic). CDP's 57 domains are bucketed into 8 categories, but only a small subset is needed to replicate human senses: vision (DOM, accessibility tree, screenshots), hearing (network traffic, console, logs), and motor control (clicks, keystrokes, navigation).

The loop escalates across rungs: synthetic JavaScript clicks (rung 1) for cases like Outlook's compose box; trusted CDP input.dispatchMouseEvent clicks (rung 2) for sites like Amazon that filter untrusted input; and rung 3, which adds human motion with jitter and dwell plus vision-based reasoning. Cloudflare Turnstile is bypassed by computing the checkbox coordinates through cross-origin iframes and closed shadow roots and firing a trusted click at that screen position. MT Captcha is solved by screenshotting the challenge and routing trusted keystrokes into the cross-origin iframe. Lemon-style drag puzzles sample the mouse trail and are defeated with a humanlike drag that eases in, deliberately overshoots, and eases back. reCAPTCHA v2 is split into a deterministic solver (trusted click, iframe piercing, grid screenshot, round rearming) and an operator agent that only inspects the grid to pick the correct tiles, with speed across multiple rounds being decisive.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.
temporalContext: Transcript claims reflect the publication date; linked external context was checked at the run's research date.
takeaways: A CDP-driven browser is, from the perspective of Google and Cloudflare, functionally equivalent to a human user, since clicks and keystrokes travel the exact same internal path.
Chrome stamps every input event as trusted or untrusted; synthetic JS clicks work in Outlook but are silently dropped by Amazon's add-to-cart button.
Choose a CLI over an MCP server: same ~83% success rate, but 7 turns vs 71 round trips, under one minute vs 8 minutes, and up to 75x cheaper in token cost.
The sense-act-verify loop only escalates when the page fights back; climb the lowest rung that works.
CDP's 57 domains can be bucketed; only a small subset covering digital senses (DOM/accessibility tree/screenshots, network/console, input) is needed for human-like browsing.
Rung 1 (synthetic JS) works where the web UI acts as a permissionless API, e.g., Outlook sending without Office 365 app registration.
Rung 3 requires both human mouse paths with jitter and dwell and vision to interpret image-based challenges.
Cloudflare Turnstile is bypassed by locating the iframe on screen and firing a trusted click at the computed checkbox coordinates; no human in the loop is needed.
Drag-puzzle captchas sample the entire mouse trail, so the agent must ease in, deliberately overshoot, and ease the piece back into the gap like a human hand.
reCAPTCHA v2 is best split into a deterministic solver (driving) and a minimal operator (one AI look per round) because every round expires on a clock.

sections.title: Threatened with a ban for preparing this talk
sections.summary: Gallon opens with a joke about teaching illegal skills and reveals that OpenAI threatened to ban his account over his web-automation research. He shows a dashboard where every captcha challenge is being cleared by an AI agent with no human in the loop and promises the audience will understand how by the end.

sections.title: The premise: a CDP browser is a meat bag with a mouse
sections.summary: He states the talk's one-slide premise: a browser driven via the Chrome DevTools Protocol is, from Google and Cloudflare's perspective, just like a human user, because the agent's clicks and keystrokes travel the same path inside Chrome that a real user's do. The rest of the talk covers three things: a CLI over MCP, the Chrome DevTools Protocol via his Chrome Agent tool, and a loop run on a ladder.

sections.title: Why a CLI beats an MCP server
sections.summary: He defends giving the agent a shell-based CLI rather than an MCP server. Citing an Arise AI study, both interfaces succeed ~83% of the time, but CLI sequences are programmable and reusable without a model in the loop, faster (7 turns vs 71 round trips, under 1 minute vs 8 minutes), and up to 75x cheaper in token cost per Anthropic. Speed is foreshadowed to matter at the end against time-limited reCAPTCHA rounds.

sections.title: The DevTools Protocol and the agent's digital senses
sections.summary: He introduces CDP, the same protocol behind the F12 DevTools panel, and notes Chrome Agent makes it easy for agents to write code that replays CDP interactions. Although CDP spans 57 domains with hundreds of methods and events, he buckets them into 8 categories and argues only a small subset is needed: digital senses for seeing (DOM, accessibility tree, screenshots), hearing (network traffic, console, logs), and operating (clicks, keystrokes, navigation).

sections.title: The loop: sense, act, verify
sections.summary: He defines the sense-act-verify loop run until the page gives in. Sensing happens through one or more channels; acting is a single click, type, or selection; verifying uses a different channel than the interaction (e.g., check network or screen, not the click itself). When the loop won't close, the page is fighting back and the agent must climb the ladder.

sections.title: The three rung ladder
sections.summary: He describes a three-rung 'meatbag ladder' climbed only as high as the page forces. Rung 1: no human behavior; a synthetic JavaScript click is the right default if the page exposes the action. Rung 2: a real CDP input.click using the exact path the user's mouse uses, which the page cannot distinguish. Rung 3: human input with a real mouse path, dwell, jitter, and vision to interpret images. The methodology is to explore by hand, climb rungs until it works, then automate by writing the path down as code or as an agent skill.

sections.title: Rung one: batch emails, and the web UI as a permissionless API
sections.summary: He demonstrates rung 1 by sending a batch of personalized emails from the Outlook web client. A synthetic JS click opens compose, programmatic fill inserts content, another synthetic click sends, and the captured sequence loops over 20-200 emails. He argues that in corporate environments where Office 365 API access requires app registration and admin approval, the web UI effectively becomes a permissionless universal API.

sections.title: Rung two: trusted clicks and the add to cart button
sections.summary: He moves to rung 2 with a 'Demon' (Amazon) storefront demo. The same JS click that worked in Outlook is silently dropped by the add-to-cart button because Chrome stamps every event as trusted or untrusted and the page filters untrusted input. Switching to CDP input.dispatchMouseEvent sends the click down the exact path the user's mouse uses, stamps it trusted, and the item drops into the cart. He notes the visible mouse cursor is added programmatically so the audience can see the inputs.

sections.title: Rung three: Cloudflare Turnstile and MT Captcha
sections.summary: Rung three is the narrow frontier where pages actively hunt for bots. Cloudflare Turnstile's checkbox is hidden under closed shadow roots and a cross-origin iframe; the solution asks the browser where the iframe sits, computes the checkbox screen position, and fires a trusted click at that coordinate. MT Captcha is solved by screenshotting the challenge, using vision to pick characters from the noise, and routing trusted keystrokes into the cross-origin iframe one character at a time; the server agrees and issues a token. He frames these as three gates built to keep agents out, all three beaten, leaving only the final boss.

sections.title: Lemon drag puzzle: human motion and mouse trail sampling
sections.summary: He demonstrates a Lemon-style jigsaw drag captcha. There is no shadow root and no cross-origin iframe; the piece is in the page. The hard part is the drag itself: these captchas sample the mouse movement into a trail of points including jitter and changing speeds. The agent eases in gently, takes a slight curve, deliberately overshoots the puzzle piece, and eases it back in, using vision to find the gap and humanlike motion to cross it. With Turnstile, MT Captcha, and Lemon defeated, only reCAPTCHA v2 remains.

sections.title: Final boss: reCAPTCHA v2, solver and operator
sections.summary: reCAPTCHA v2 is split into two halves. The solver is pure deterministic code: it does the trusted click on the checkbox, pierces the challenge iframe, screenshots the grid every round, and rearms itself if a round expires. The only step code cannot do is look at the grid and figure out what is in it, so the operator agent takes one look, picks the correct tiles, hands the answer back, and waits for the next round. The live demo solves the grid, and the agent spots bicycles in tiles the human missed. Speed is decisive because every round expires and challenges span multiple rounds; an agent that roundtrips a model on every click loses the clock. The takeaway is the methodology: give the agent a CLI, drive the browser through CDP, run it as a loop on the meatbag ladder, climb only as high as forced, and write the solution down. OpenAI rescinded the ban threat, and the speaker invites the audience to try Chrome Agent in the Python ecosystem or build their own.

demonstrations: Outlook web: synthetic JavaScript click opens compose, fills, and sends a batch of personalized emails without Office 365 app registration.
Amazon-style 'Demon' storefront: synthetic JS click on add-to-cart is dropped silently; trusted CDP input.click succeeds.
Cloudflare Turnstile bypassed by computing checkbox screen coordinates from the cross-origin iframe and firing a trusted click at that position.
MT Captcha: agent screenshots the challenge, uses vision to pick characters from the noise, and types the answer as trusted keystrokes into the cross-origin iframe.
Lemon drag puzzle: agent uses vision to find the gap, then drags with a humanlike curve, deliberate overshoot, and ease-back; the puzzle's mouse-trail sampling accepts the motion.
reCAPTCHA v2 solved end-to-end: deterministic code taps the checkbox, pierces the iframe, screenshots each grid, rearms on expiry, and the agent takes one look per round to pick the correct tiles.
limitations: Rung three is described as 'the narrow frontier where pages are actively hunting for bots' and requires continuous technique updates.
Synthetic JS clicks are stamped untrusted and silently dropped by pages that check input trust, as with Amazon's add-to-cart.
Cloudflare Turnstile's checkbox is hidden beneath closed shadow roots and a cross-origin iframe, making it unreachable through typical automation.
Drag-puzzle captchas sample the entire mouse path, so simple coordinate drags will be rejected.
reCAPTCHA rounds expire, and an agent that roundtrips a model on every click and look burns the clock and loses the challenge.
OpenAI initially threatened to ban the speaker's account for this research before rescinding the warning after a conversation.
quantitativeClaims: Arise AI study: CLI and MCP both succeed at ~83% on the same task.
CLI: 7 turns, under 1 minute; MCP: 71 round trips, 8 minutes for the same task.
Anthropic reported CLI can be up to 75x cheaper in token cost than MCP.
CDP exposes 57 domains with hundreds of methods and events; the speaker buckets them into 8 categories.
Outlook batch email demo loops over 20-200 emails from a single captured command sequence.
reCAPTCHA rounds expire on a clock, and a challenge can be multiple rounds back to back, making per-round speed decisive.

evidence.supports: Core premise that CDP-driven agents are indistinguishable from human users to bot-detection vendors.

evidence.excerpt: in that same study that I mentioned before, MCP took 71 round trips and 8 minutes for the same task that took a CLI only seven turns and in under one minute.
evidence.supports: CLI speed advantage over MCP for the same ~83% capability.

evidence.excerpt: Anthropic themselves reported that the CLI can be as much as 75 times cheaper in terms of token cost.
Chrome stamps every single event with just that answer whether it's trusted or untrusted. So the JavaScript click that we fired previously is stamped untrusted.
evidence.supports: Mechanism by which synthetic JS clicks are silently dropped on Amazon's add-to-cart.

evidence.excerpt: We ask the browser where it is that the iframe sits on the screen. We do a little bit of math to figure out where the checkbox is. Then we fire a trusted click right at that position on the glass
evidence.supports: Rung 3 technique for defeating Cloudflare Turnstile without human involvement.

evidence.excerpt: uses its own vision capability to pick the characters out of the noise. Then it types the answer back using real trusted keystrokes routed into the widgets cross origin iframe one character at a time
evidence.supports: MT Captcha technique using vision plus trusted keystrokes into the cross-origin iframe.

evidence.excerpt: It actually deliberately overshoots the puzzle piece and then eases it right back in just like a meat bag with a mouse.
evidence.supports: Humanlike drag motion with deliberate overshoot defeats mouse-trail-sampling drag captchas.

evidence.excerpt: This is pure code. No agent, no model. It does everything programmatically. It does the trusted click in the checkbox. It pierces into the challenge iframe
evidence.supports: The solver half of the reCAPTCHA v2 system is deterministic code with no model in the loop.

evidence.excerpt: the only thing that we give the agent as a job. We call that bit the operator. The solver taps the agent on the shoulder and the agent takes one look at the grid
evidence.supports: The operator/agent is invoked only to inspect the grid and pick tiles; everything else is deterministic.

evidence.excerpt: Every round expires and one challenge can be multiple rounds back to back. An agent that roundtrips a model on every click and on every look burns that clock and loses.
evidence.supports: Per-round speed, not capability, is what defeats reCAPTCHA v2.
